title: After an 8-Year Journey, Orbiters Are About to Give Us a Fresh Look at Mercury - Nautilus
gist: The ESA/JAXA BepiColombo twin orbiters have arrived at Mercury after launching on October 20, 2018, with an unexpected 2024 glitch having forced a rerouting that delayed arrival by more than six months.

insights.claim: The BepiColombo twin orbiters, built by the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched on October 20, 2018 and have now arrived at Mercury, the solar system’s smallest planet.
insights.so_what: An eight-year cruise between launch and first science illustrates the capital-cycle length agencies and their contractors must underwrite for inner-solar-system missions.
insights.locator: The BepiColombo twin orbiters built by the European Space Agency
insights.speaker: David Nield

insights.claim: BepiColombo is not the first spacecraft to visit Mercury, so its value lies in improved instruments rather than first access.
insights.so_what: Repeat-visit missions are justified on instrument generation gains, which is where the supplier value accrues.
insights.quote: But the BepiColombo twin orbiters aren’t the first spacecraft to visit our system’s smallest planet.
insights.locator: But the BepiColombo twin orbiters aren’t the first spacecraft
insights.speaker: David Nield

insights.claim: An unexpected glitch in 2024 forced the conjoined BepiColombo spacecraft to take a different route to Mercury, delaying arrival by more than six months and leaving the craft "a little worse for wear."
insights.so_what: Trajectory replanning can absorb hardware faults but not without multi-quarter schedule slip — a concrete measure of program risk on long-duration missions.
insights.quote: An unexpected glitch back in 2024 forced the conjoined spacecraft to take a different route to Mercury, delaying its arrival by more than six months
insights.speaker: David Nield
